rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window for all eight compounds while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained peaks. This run will identify critical pairs and guide subsequent window, slope, and temperature adjustments.
Keep the gradient unchanged and raise temperature to test selectivity of the only unresolved pair. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, preserving the zero time penalty.

Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. This tests whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5 under modestly increased steepness.

Reduce the gradient slope to lie between injections 2 and 3, aiming to restore the critical pair to R ≥ 1.5 while remaining faster than injection 2. The lower endpoint is still well above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 4's slope to test whether retention can be shortened without losing full resolution. The first peaks previously eluted near 0.18 organic fraction, so a 0.10 starting fraction leaves some focusing margin.

With a maximum-score method already established, test a lower-temperature selectivity regime using a faster gradient. Cooling may reverse and separate the critical early pair, potentially allowing full resolution at a steeper slope.

Raise temperature one step from injection 6 to split the late coeluting cluster while testing whether the early pair remains resolved. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates the temperature-selectivity response.

Test a higher starting fraction at 35 C to seek a faster, fully resolved low-temperature method. Warming should spread the late cluster, while the shifted window and shallower slope may compensate for reduced early-pair selectivity.

Return to the successful 60 C selectivity and use a slope just steeper than injection 4 to seek a slightly faster maximum-score method. The 0.70 endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, while the critical pair is expected to retain R ≥ 1.5.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 9, targeting the fastest gradient that preserves early-pair resolution. The last peak may enter the final hold, so this run will establish whether the lower endpoint offsets the speed gain.

Test whether a shallower slope can restore the early-pair resolution lost when the starting fraction was raised in injection 5. This probes an alternative maximum-score window, with all peaks expected to elute well before 10 minutes.

With the maximum CRF secured, test a more robust fully resolved method by flattening the gradient at 60 C. The early pair should gain separation while the last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes; monitor the narrowing third–fourth pair.

Flatten injection 8's gradient while retaining its starting fraction and temperature to improve the unresolved early pair. This tests whether the cooler selectivity regime can also achieve maximum CRF, with the last peak expected before 10 minutes.

Lower injection 13's endpoint one grid step to bring the early pair above R = 1.5 through a modest slope reduction. The last peak is expected around 9.3 minutes, leaving room to reach maximum CRF without a time penalty.

With maximum CRF already secured, test whether a higher starting fraction can produce a faster resolved method in the cooler selectivity regime. The narrower gradient may spread the late cluster, but this run also checks whether early retention remains sufficient.

Test the remaining slope boundary between the fully resolved injection 10 and the slightly unresolved injection 3. The higher endpoint keeps the last peak inside the gradient and may deliver a faster maximum-score method, although early-pair resolution is near its limit.

Refine the higher-starting-fraction branch with a slope slightly steeper than injection 11, targeting R near 1.5 and a shorter retention time. This is a new grid method that may retain maximum CRF while narrowing the speed boundary.

Test a further upward shift of the starting fraction, compensated by a shallower gradient to protect early-pair resolution. This checks whether the higher-starting-fraction branch offers another fully resolved, sub-10-minute method.

With maximum CRF already secured, seek greater resolution margin by flattening the successful 0.10-start gradient. The last peak is expected near 9.6 minutes, potentially allowing stronger early-pair separation without a time penalty.

Lengthen the fastest fully resolved method, injection 10, by one step to gain resolution margin while keeping the gradient endpoint near the last peak’s elution fraction. This should retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient than the other high-margin methods.

Increase injection 20’s endpoint one grid step to shorten retention while retaining more resolution margin than the fastest method. The resulting slope lies between two successful slopes, so all pairs are expected to remain fully resolved.

Lower injection 10’s endpoint one step to improve early-pair resolution while retaining a six-minute programmed gradient. The last peak will elute during the hold; test whether it still arrives before 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF with lower organic consumption.

Increase injection 21’s endpoint one step to shorten retention while preserving full resolution. This reproduces injection 2’s successful slope with a trimmed window, and the last peak should elute inside the gradient near 7.5 minutes.

Trim the successful higher-starting-fraction method to an eight-minute gradient, with a slightly shallower slope than injection 11 to preserve full resolution. The last peak should remain inside the gradient near 7.3 minutes, maintaining maximum CRF.

Trim injection 24 to a six-minute gradient with a slightly shallower slope to preserve early-pair resolution, testing whether the final hold still permits maximum CRF. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, with the last peak at 6.97 minutes.
